title: The Lord is my light (Psalm 26 [27])
hookLine: whom shall I fear, and one thing I ask, to dwell in his house

cards: A kid in a dark bedroom. The door is half open. The coat on the chair has become a person.
Every sound in the house is a footstep. Then someone flips on the hall light, and the coat is just a coat. Nothing in the room changed.
Only the light did. Adults have their own dark rooms: the test results, the layoff rumor, the phone that rings at two in the morning.
Psalm 26 in the Douay, 27 in most Bibles, walks straight into that room and turns on the light.

teach.b: It opens with a question that's almost a dare: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?" It doesn't say there's nothing out there.
The next lines are full of enemies, armies camped around, war rising up. The light doesn't make the danger vanish. It shows who's with you in it.
Then the heart of the psalm, a single wish: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life."
Out of everything a frightened person might ask for, safety, victory, money, it asks for one thing: to be near God, at home. And it doesn't stay brave the whole way.
Halfway through, the voice cracks: don't hide your face from me, don't turn away.

teach.h: FATHER AND MOTHER HAVE LEFT ME.
teach.b: Then: "For my father and my mother have left me: but the Lord hath taken me up."

It ends not with a feeling but with an instruction to itself: "Expect the Lord, do manfully, and let thy heart take courage, and wait thou for the Lord." Courage here isn't the absence of fear. It's waiting anyway.

The Latin first words, Dominus illuminatio mea, are the motto of the University of Oxford, printed on its open book. Jews pray it too: by custom, it's said daily through the season of the High Holy Days.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 26 [27] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass and at funerals, where its line 'one thing I have asked' is often chosen.

o: my light, the light that shows who's with you
my bread, the food that keeps you going
my fear, the dread that comes in the dark

p: to dwell in the house of the Lord

s: the psalm says there is nothing to be afraid of

games.q: out of everything a frightened person could ask God for, what is the one thing the psalm asks?
o: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.
games.why: one thing I have asked of the Lord: to dwell in his house. not safety or victory first, but nearness.

practice: Find the fear sitting closest to you today, the one that turns coats into people, name it plainly in a few words, and picture setting it on the floor beside you like a heavy bag: still there, just not in your hands for now.
If you pray, say: the Lord is my light, whom shall I fear? If you don't, simply breathe beside it.
